city: East Rutherford, New Jersey (New York/New Jersey metro)
primary_tenant: New York Giants and New York Jets (NFL)
architect: 360 Architecture (lead); EwingCole (per Wikipedia rev 1360702806, listed alongside Rockwell Group and Bruce Mau Design)

capacity_wc2026_source.title: FIFA World Cup 2026 stadium capacities confirmed (FIFA, 10 June 2026)

field_type_2026: Natural grass (Bermudagrass) installed on modular trays over existing FieldTurf infrastructure; sand base, irrigation, and ventilation layers topped by ~600 rolls of turf to form a 105 x 68 m FIFA pitch. Converted from artificial turf specifically for the World Cup; Bermudagrass first installed early May 2026 (per ESPN).
renovation_cost_2026: Over US$100 million in World Cup-readiness upgrades, privately funded by Giants/Jets ownership, on top of the original ~US$1.6 billion construction cost; per meetstadium.com (single outlet, not an itemized/FIFA-audited figure).

iconic_games.note: Chile retained the Copa América on penalties (attendance 82,026 per Wikipedia). Lionel Messi missed his penalty and subsequently announced a (temporary) retirement from international football. Score, teams and shootout result confirmed against the cited Wikipedia revision.
Lionel Messi scored a hat-trick including the late winner. 4–3 Argentina, Messi hat-trick confirmed against Wikipedia rev and ESPN match report (gameId 337320).

Portugal beat Ireland 5–1 (listed Ireland-first as 1–5). Cristiano Ronaldo started in Portugal's final World Cup warm-up. Confirmed against Wikipedia rev ('Portugal beating Ireland 5–1') and ESPN match report (gameId 364825).

iconic_games_note: MetLife has genuine top-tier football history: it hosted the 2016 Copa América Centenario final (Chile beat Argentina 4–2 on penalties after 0–0) and numerous marquee international friendlies — Argentina 4–3 Brazil (2012, Messi hat-trick, ESPN gameId 337320); Portugal 5–1 Ireland (2014, ESPN gameId 364825); Brazil 1–0 Ecuador (Sep 9 2014, ESPN gameId 405991, Willian goal — independently verified by this fact-check). NON-football note (clearly labelled): it hosted Super Bowl XLVIII (Feb 2, 2014, Seattle 43, Denver 8) — the first cold-weather, open-air Super Bowl (game-time temp ~49°F); East Rutherford is the smallest municipality ever to host a Super Bowl. In 2026 it hosts the World Cup final (July 19, 2026).

renovations.change: Two-phase lower-bowl renovation: the four corners of the precast concrete seating bowl were demolished and rebuilt with a new modular steel-composite seating system; an additional 1,740 permanent corner seats were replaced with the modular system (removable for the wider FIFA pitch). Wikipedia indicates NFL capacity was maintained. Phase I completed May 2024; Phase II completed May 2025. The 1,740 figure is corroborated by ESPN ('a total of 1,740 seats from the corners had to be removed').

Conversion from artificial turf to natural Bermudagrass on modular trays for the World Cup. Build-up over existing turf infrastructure includes a sand base, permeable cloth and ventilation layers, topped by ~600 rolls of turf to form a 105 x 68 m FIFA-regulation pitch. Bermudagrass first installed early May 2026. Confirmed against ESPN (600 rolls, Bermuda grass, 105x68m, early-May install).

renovations.change: Broader World Cup-readiness upgrades (over US$100M, privately funded, single-outlet): concourse, WiFi/cellular, broadcast/media, accessibility, exterior arrival areas, and FIFA-required security/technology/branding changes (corporate name suspended to 'New York New Jersey Stadium' during the tournament).

city_history.founded: East Rutherford, NJ incorporated as a borough March 28, 1894 (from Boiling Springs Township). The Meadowlands Sports Complex opened in 1976; MetLife Stadium opened in 2010.
city_history.significance: East Rutherford is a small Bergen County borough (~7 miles west of Midtown Manhattan) anchored by the Meadowlands Sports Complex — home to MetLife Stadium, the Meadowlands Racetrack and the American Dream mega-mall. It is the smallest municipality ever to host a Super Bowl (XLVIII, 2014) and hosts the 2026 World Cup final.
city_history.football_culture: Hung on the New York/New Jersey metropolitan area, not the borough. The NY/NJ metro is one of the largest, most football-passionate U.S. markets: New York Red Bulls and NYCFC (MLS), the historic 1970s-80s New York Cosmos (Pelé, Beckenbauer), and vast Latino, European and African diaspora fanbases. MetLife/Giants Stadium has a long record of selling out marquee internationals (Copa América Centenario final, Argentina–Brazil superclásicos). The 'New York New Jersey' WC branding reflects the bi-state market. Correctly attributed to the metro, not the small borough.

stadium_history_facts: Opened April 10, 2010 as New Meadowlands Stadium; renamed MetLife Stadium under a 25-year naming-rights deal signed August 23, 2011 (per Wikipedia rev 1360702806).
Built at ~US$1.6 billion, privately financed by the Giants and Jets ownership — the most expensive stadium in the U.S. at the time of completion.
Owned via the New Jersey Sports and Exposition Authority lineage; replaced Giants Stadium (1976–2010) on the Meadowlands Sports Complex.
Shared home of two NFL teams, the New York Giants and New York Jets.
Designed by 360 Architecture (lead), with EwingCole, Rockwell Group and Bruce Mau Design; neutral exterior lighting in each home team's colors.
Hosted Super Bowl XLVIII (Feb 2, 2014, Seattle 43 Denver 8) — the first cold-weather, open-air Super Bowl (~49°F at kickoff).
Hosted the 2016 Copa América Centenario final (Chile beat Argentina 4–2 on penalties).
Selected by FIFA to host the 2026 World Cup final on July 19, 2026; hosts 8 matches total (5 group, 1 R32, 1 R16, the final) — schedule independently confirmed.
Playing surface converted from artificial turf to natural Bermudagrass for the 2026 World Cup.
